etymologies.etymologyHTML: Borrowed from Latin ēvolvō (“unroll, unfold”), from ē- (“out of”) (short form of ex) + volvō (“roll”).

definitions.definition: To move (something) in regular procession through a system.

quote.citation: a. 1677 (date written), Matthew Hale, The Primitive Origination of Mankind, Considered and Examined According to the Light of Nature, London:  […]  William Godbid, for William Shrowsbery, […], published 1677, →OCLC:
quote.text: The animal soul sooner expands and evolves it self to its full orb and extent than the humane Soul

definitions.definition: To cause (something) to come into being or develop.

quote.citation: 1939, P. G. Wodehouse, Uncle Fred in the Springtime:
quote.text: You will remove the pig, place it in the car, and drive it to my house in Wiltshire. That is the plan I have evolved.

quote.citation: 1979 August 25, Vicki Gabriner, Susan Freundlich, “Bridging the Gaps between Deaf and Hearing Lesbians”, in Gay Community News, volume 7, number 6, page 8:
quote.text: The interpreter has spent a whole lot of time working the music before the performance, trying to evolve the most accurate translation possible.

quote.citation: 2005, Donald Keene, quoting Emperor Kōmei, Emperor of Japan: Meiji and His world, 1852–1912‎[1], New York: Columbia University Press, →ISBN, →OCLC, chapter 9, page 78:
quote.text: […] I ask you, rather, to evolve a suitable plan with due deliberation and report it to me."14

definitions.definition: Of a population: to acquire or develop (a trait) in the process of biological evolution.

quote.citation: 2013 September-October, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist‎[2], archived from the original on 3 September 2013:
quote.text: Oxygen levels on Earth skyrocketed 2.4 billion years ago, when cyanobacteria evolved photosynthesis: the ability to convert water and carbon dioxide into carbohydrates and waste oxygen using solar energy.

definitions.definition: (chiefly passive voice) To cause (a population, a species, etc.) to change genetic composition over successive generations through the process of evolution.

quote.citation: 1859 November 24, Charles Darwin, “Recapitulation and Conclusion”, in On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, […], London: John Murray, […], →OCLC, page 490:
quote.text: There is grandeur in this view of life, with its several powers, having been originally breathed into a few forms or into one; and that, whilst this planet has gone cycling on according to the fixed law of gravity, from so simple a beginning endless forms most beautiful and most wonderful have been, and are being, evolved.

quote.citation: 2018, Tim Flannery, Europe: A Natural History, page 204:
quote.text: The ice age was nearly two million years old by the time the woolly mammoth evolved.

definitions.definition: (chemistry) To give off (a gas such as carbon dioxide or oxygen) during a chemical reaction.

quote.citation: [1795], James Woodhouse, “[To William Shenstone, Esq. in His Sickness.] Elegy VI. To a Lady, on the Language of the Birds.”, in William Shenstone, The Poetical Works of William Shenstone. […], Cooke’s edition, London:  […]  C. Cooke, […], →OCLC, page 54, lines 9–12:
quote.text: And come, my Muſe! that lov'ſt the ſylvan ſhade, / Evolve the mazes, and the miſt diſpel; / Tranſlate the ſong; convince my doubting maid / No ſolemn Derviſe can explain ſo vvell—  […]

definitions.definition: To move in regular procession through a system.

quote.citation: 1840, William Whewell, “Of Art and Science”, in The Philosophy of the Inductive Sciences, Founded upon Their History. […], volume II, London: John W[illiam] Parker, […]; Cambridge, Cambridgeshire: J. and J. J. Deighton, →OCLC, part II (Of Knowledge), book XI (Of the Construction of Science), paragraph 6, page 275:
quote.text: [T]he principles which Art involves, Science alone evolves.
Not by any power evolved from man's own resources, but by a power which descended from above.

definitions.definition: (biology) Of a trait; to develop within a population through biological evolution.
